title: Generations, SOH, and LOH
hook: Most objects die young. The CLR bets on that with three generations on the small object heap, and a side door — the large object heap — for buffers that would be expensive to shuffle.

sections.heading: Generational hypothesis on the SOH
sections.prose: New small objects are generation 0. A gen-0 collection inspects only the nursery plus remembered references from older generations. Survivors promote to gen 1, then gen 2. Gen 0 and 1 are ephemeral. A gen-2 collection is a full GC: all generations, including the LOH (sometimes called generation 3 physically, collected logically with gen 2). Workstation GC uses a single heap and is tuned for UI latency. Server GC allocates a heap per logical processor so a 8-core API process can allocate in parallel and collect with more GC threads. ASP.NET Core on .NET 10 defaults to server GC. In a tiny sidecar container, workstation GC can use less memory. Do not recite segment sizes from an old table as constants; Microsoft documents them as implementation details that change.

snippets.label: SOH versus LOH in a CSV buffer
snippets.explanation: 64 KiB stays on the SOH (under 85,000 bytes). A 200 KiB row buffer is LOH: gen-2 lifetime tax and fragmentation risk.

sections.heading: Large object heap rules of thumb
sections.prose: The default LOH threshold is 85,000 bytes. Double arrays can land on the LOH slightly below that because of alignment; interviews usually want ‘about 85 KB.’ LOH objects are not compacted on every collection because memmove of megabytes is expensive. Free holes remain. A Redis payload cache that allocates a new 200 KB byte[] per miss will fragment. ArrayPool<byte>.Shared, recycle buffers, or compact LOH explicitly (GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode) when you must. Container hard limits can force LOH compaction. Server versus workstation does not change the 85 KB rule; it changes how many heaps and how pauses are scheduled (background GC versus blocking).

interviewTakeaways: Gen 0 is frequent and cheap; gen 2 is the pause you feel in a service.
LOH ≈ 85 KB+, collected with gen 2, compacted only when configured or under hard limits.
Server GC is one heap per CPU for throughput; workstation is the desktop default.
commonPitfalls: Allocating one giant string or byte[] per CSV file in a request.
Calling GC.Collect(2) to ‘clean the LOH’ in production.
Assuming server GC always has shorter pauses (it often has higher throughput and different pause shapes).

jsTsCorrelations.note: V8 also uses a nursery (new space) and old space. There is no official 85 KB LOH switch you set in app code; large typed arrays are handled separately from JS objects.
